items.stem: Define the term "extended metaphor".
items.answer: A metaphor that is continued over several lines or a whole poem
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a metaphor that is continued over several lines or a whole poem. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem:
Read the following sequence of three haiku, "Monsoon Morning".

First fat drops of rain –
the dusty street holds its breath,
then the whole sky falls.

Children in puddles
splash the grey world into gold –
school bags overhead.

Evening. Frogs begin
their loud green orchestra; the
drains sing all night long.

Identify the technique used in "the whole sky falls" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Hyperbole: "the whole sky falls" – the exaggeration conveys the sudden, overwhelming force of monsoon rain.
items.markingKey: Hyperbole: "the whole sky falls" – the exaggeration conveys the sudden, overwhelming force of monsoon rain. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Any sentence with "like" in it is a simile." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: "Like" must introduce a comparison; "I like pizza" uses "like" as a verb and is not a simile.
items.markingKey: "Like" must introduce a comparison; "I like pizza" uses "like" as a verb and is not a simile. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a simile and a metaphor to describe a busy school corridor.
items.answer: Any valid pair, e.g. simile: "Students poured through the corridor like a river in flood." Metaphor: "The corridor was a beehive at the bell." 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Any valid pair, e.g. simile: "Students poured through the corridor like a river in flood." Metaphor: "The corridor was a beehive at the bell." 1 mark each.

items.stem:
Read the following poem by a student poet, "My Grandmother's Hands".

Her hands are maps of seventy years,
rivers of blue beneath brown paper skin.
They knead the dough like they are
pressing out the war, the boat, the cold.
Flour rises like snow in reverse.
When she holds mine, I feel the journey –
every border folded into her palms.

Explain the effect of the simile "They knead the dough like they are / pressing out the war, the boat, the cold" on the reader.
items.answer: Simile: "They knead the dough like they are / pressing out the war, the boat, the cold" – the everyday task of baking becomes a way of working through painful memories of migration.
items.markingKey: Simile: "They knead the dough like they are / pressing out the war, the boat, the cold" – the everyday task of baking becomes a way of working through painful memories of migration. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Identify the device in each: (a) "The classroom was a zoo." (b) "The leaves danced in the wind." (c) "As quiet as a held breath."
items.answer: (a) metaphor; (b) personification; (c) simile.
items.markingKey: (a) metaphor; (b) personification; (c) simile.

items.stem:

How does the poet use imagery to present the grandmother and her past?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The extended map metaphor ("maps of seventy years", "every border folded into her palms") presents her hands as a record of a journey across borders. The speaker's touch ("When she holds mine") passes the history on.

items.stem: Explain why an extended metaphor can be more powerful than a single metaphor.
items.answer: Developing one comparison across a poem builds layers of meaning and gives the poem unity, as with the hands-as-maps image that returns in "every border folded into her palms".

items.stem: "Figurative language makes poetry harder to understand, so it should be used sparingly." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Figurative language usually makes poems more vivid and memorable; the skill is choosing precise images rather than piling them up.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: too many images can confuse; plain language can be powerful. Arguments against: images make abstract feelings concrete; readers remember vivid images. Supported judgement: Figurative language usually makes poems more vivid and memorable; the skill is choosing precise images rather than piling them up. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line, which creates a beat"?
items.answer: rhythm
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of rhythm.

items.stem: Distinguish between alliteration and assonance.
items.answer: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds at the start of words ("crooked crag"); assonance repeats vowel sounds inside words ("the light of the fire is a sight").
items.markingKey: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds at the start of words ("crooked crag"); assonance repeats vowel sounds inside words ("the light of the fire is a sight"). The city does not sleep;

a generator heart
beating under every street.
Danfo buses honk like geese.
A radio somewhere
is singing to nobody,
and the moon,
tired of competing,
hides behind the billboards.

Describe the tone of the text and explain how the writer creates it.
items.answer: The tone is energetic and affectionate: lively sound images and humour show love for the busy city.
items.markingKey: The tone is energetic and affectionate: lively sound images and humour show love for the busy city. items.stem: A student claims: "Alliteration means words start with the same letter." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Alliteration is about the same sound: "cat" and "kite" alliterate, but "city" and "cat" do not.
items.markingKey: Alliteration is about the same sound: "cat" and "kite" alliterate, but "city" and "cat" do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a line of poetry about rain that includes onomatopoeia and alliteration.
items.answer: Any line with both, e.g. "Pitter-patter, puddles plop on the path." 1 mark each device.
items.markingKey: Any line with both, e.g. "Pitter-patter, puddles plop on the path." 1 mark each device.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Sound devices matter more when a poem is read aloud than when it is read silently."
items.answer: Sound devices are strongest aloud, but they shape meaning and mood even when a poem is read silently.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rhythm and rhyme are heard; spoken word depends on sound. Arguments against: readers "hear" sounds in their heads; sound devices also link ideas on the page. Supported judgement: Sound devices are strongest aloud, but they shape meaning and mood even when a poem is read silently.

items.stem: A poem rhymes AABBA. Which form is this most likely to be?
items.answer: A limerick
items.markingKey: A. Limericks have five lines rhyming AABBA.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "ballad".
items.answer: A poem that tells a story, usually in four-line stanzas with a regular rhythm and rhyme, often with repetition
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a poem that tells a story, usually in four-line stanzas with a regular rhythm and rhyme, often with repetition. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem:
Read the following limerick by a student poet.

A girl from the top of Peru
Had a llama that sang in the zoo.
When the crowd shouted, "Stop!"
It hit a high top,
And the keeper joined in with it too.

Identify the form of this poem and describe two of its features.
items.answer: It is a limerick: five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme (Peru/zoo/too; Stop/top), a bouncing rhythm with longer lines 1, 2 and 5 and shorter lines 3 and 4, and a humorous, absurd story.
items.markingKey: It is a limerick: five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme (Peru/zoo/too; Stop/top), a bouncing rhythm with longer lines 1, 2 and 5 and shorter lines 3 and 4, and a humorous, absurd story. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.answer: Reading silently lets the reader go at their own pace and reread; performance uses voice, pace, volume and gesture to interpret the poem for an audience in real time.

items.answer: A simile compares using "like" or "as" ("honk like geese"); a metaphor states that one thing is another ("a generator heart"), which is usually a stronger, more direct comparison.

items.stem:
Read the following spoken-word poem performed by a 14-year-old at a youth festival in London.

They call us the screen generation.
Screen – like something you hide behind.
Screen – like something you sieve the truth through.
But I am not a screen.
I am a voice
and I am LOUD,
and I have been waiting fourteen years
for you to hear me say it:
we see more than you think.

Explain how you would perform this poem aloud, referring to pace, volume, pauses and gesture.
items.answer: Spoken-word performance: build volume from a calm opening to a shout on "LOUD", pause before the final line, make eye contact on "you" and use a gesture (pointing to the eyes) on "we see more than you think".
items.markingKey: Spoken-word performance: build volume from a calm opening to a shout on "LOUD", pause before the final line, make eye contact on "you" and use a gesture (pointing to the eyes) on "we see more than you think". Read the following extract from a short story with a twist ending.

Every night that week, Sam heard footsteps following her home from the bus stop. Every night she walked faster. Every night she didn't look back.
On Friday she couldn't bear it. At the corner she spun round, fists raised.
A small boy in a yellow raincoat stopped dead. He was holding out her purse.
'You dropped it on Monday,' he whispered. 'I've been trying to catch up.'

Identify the device in the quotation "fists raised. / A small boy in a yellow raincoat".
items.answer: contrast

items.stem: Distinguish between a metaphor and a simile.
items.answer: A simile compares using "like" or "as" ("honk like geese"); a metaphor states that one thing is another ("a generator heart"), which is usually a stronger, more direct comparison.
items.markingKey: A simile compares using "like" or "as" ("honk like geese"); a metaphor states that one thing is another ("a generator heart"), which is usually a stronger, more direct comparison. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why poets use rhythm and rhyme.
items.answer: They make poems musical and memorable, help them be performed aloud, and can link important words or create humour.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They make poems musical and memorable, help them be performed aloud, and can link important words or create humour. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following limerick by a student poet.

A girl from the top of Peru
Had a llama that sang in the zoo.
When the crowd shouted, "Stop!"
It hit a high top,
And the keeper joined in with it too.

What poetic form is used here? Give two pieces of evidence.
items.answer: It is a limerick: five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme (Peru/zoo/too; Stop/top), a bouncing rhythm with longer lines 1, 2 and 5 and shorter lines 3 and 4, and a humorous, absurd story.
items.markingKey: It is a limerick: five lines with an AABBA rhyme scheme (Peru/zoo/too; Stop/top), a bouncing rhythm with longer lines 1, 2 and 5 and shorter lines 3 and 4, and a humorous, absurd story. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following ballad by a student poet, "The Ferryman's Daughter".

The river ran both wide and black,
The storm came down the hill;
The ferryman went out at dusk
And has not come back still.

His daughter took the lantern down
And walked into the rain;
She called his name across the waves –
She called and called again.

Explain how you would perform this poem aloud, referring to pace, volume, pauses and gesture.
items.answer: Read slowly with a steady rhythm, lower the voice for the dark setting, and let the repetition grow louder or more desperate on "called and called again"; in a choral reading, different voices could echo "called".
items.markingKey: Read slowly with a steady rhythm, lower the voice for the dark setting, and let the repetition grow louder or more desperate on "called and called again"; in a choral reading, different voices could echo "called". Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following sequence of three haiku, "Monsoon Morning".

First fat drops of rain –
the dusty street holds its breath,
then the whole sky falls.

Children in puddles
splash the grey world into gold –
school bags overhead.

Evening. Frogs begin
their loud green orchestra; the
drains sing all night long.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in "splash the grey world into gold".
items.answer: Colour imagery: "splash the grey world into gold" – the change from grey to gold shows how the children's joy transforms the scene.
items.markingKey: Colour imagery: "splash the grey world into gold" – the change from grey to gold shows how the children's joy transforms the scene. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "All poems must rhyme." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many poems, including free verse and most haiku, do not rhyme; poets choose whether rhyme suits their purpose.
items.markingKey: Many poems, including free verse and most haiku, do not rhyme; poets choose whether rhyme suits their purpose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following spoken-word poem performed by a 14-year-old at a youth festival in London.

They call us the screen generation.
Screen – like something you hide behind.
Screen – like something you sieve the truth through.
But I am not a screen.
I am a voice
and I am LOUD,
and I have been waiting fourteen years
for you to hear me say it:
we see more than you think.

Explain how the form of this poem suits its subject and purpose.
items.answer: It is a spoken-word poem written in free verse for performance: it uses repetition, direct address and changes in volume (capitals on "LOUD") to work on a live audience.
items.markingKey: It is a spoken-word poem written in free verse for performance: it uses repetition, direct address and changes in volume (capitals on "LOUD") to work on a live audience. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following free verse poem by a student poet, "Lagos at Midnight".

The city does not sleep;
it hums,
a generator heart
beating under every street.
Danfo buses honk like geese.
A radio somewhere
is singing to nobody,
and the moon,
tired of competing,
hides behind the billboards.

Explain how you would perform this poem aloud, referring to pace, volume, pauses and gesture.
items.answer: Perform with varied pace: slow and quiet for "it hums," faster and louder for the honking buses, and a soft, playful voice for the hiding moon; spoken-word style suits it.
items.markingKey: Perform with varied pace: slow and quiet for "it hums," faster and louder for the honking buses, and a soft, playful voice for the hiding moon; spoken-word style suits it. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following free verse poem by a student poet, "Lagos at Midnight".

The city does not sleep;
it hums,
a generator heart
beating under every street.
Danfo buses honk like geese.
A radio somewhere
is singing to nobody,
and the moon,
tired of competing,
hides behind the billboards.

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the poet use imagery and sound to present Lagos at night?
items.answer: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "Sound devices matter more when a poem is read aloud than when it is read silently." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Sound devices are strongest aloud, but they shape meaning and mood even when a poem is read silently.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rhythm and rhyme are heard; spoken word depends on sound. Arguments against: readers "hear" sounds in their heads; sound devices also link ideas on the page. Supported judgement: Sound devices are strongest aloud, but they shape meaning and mood even when a poem is read silently. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "Strict poetic forms limit a poet's creativity." Discuss.
items.answer: Forms can both limit and inspire; many poets find that constraints sharpen their creativity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rules restrict word choice; free verse allows more freedom. Arguments against: constraints push poets to be inventive; form can add meaning (e.g. a ballad's song-like repetition).
